query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a modest amount of HCP‐forming elements (e.g. Ti, Zr or Hf) into a predominantly BCC refractory high-entropy alloy (such as VNbMoTaW) will improve its strength–plasticity combination by modifying dislocation core properties and increasing lattice distortion.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, fully BCC refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., VNbMoTaW) known to exhibit high strength but very low ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Alloy the BCC RHEA with a controlled addition (e.g., ~10–20 at.%) of HCP-forming refractory elements (such as Ti, Zr, or Hf).
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical testing (compression/tension), ensuring the modified alloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
generation.structural_mediator: Alteration of the dislocation core characteristics by lowering the dislocation core energy and increasing lattice distortion; a shift in the balance between screw and edge dislocation mobilities.
generation.mechanism: The introduced HCP elements disrupt the pure BCC lattice, reducing shear modulus locally and modifying the dislocation core structure. This can activate additional slip systems or alter slip plane preferences, thereby enhancing plasticity while still retaining high yield strength due to solid solution and lattice distortion strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the pure BCC alloy, the modified alloy is expected to exhibit improved ductility (increased plastic strain before failure) and maintain or slightly enhance yield strength, yielding a more balanced strength–plasticity combination.
generation.baseline: The unmodified BCC RHEA (e.g., VNbMoTaW) which shows high strength but negligible room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to hold for moderate additions of HCP-forming elements; excessive incorporation may lead to secondary phase formation or unwanted degradation of high-temperature creep properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement levels (quantitative changes in yield strength and plastic strain) remain uncertain and require experimental optimization; trade-offs at different temperatures are also possible.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys: a control set of pure VNbMoTaW and a test set of VNbMoTaW alloyed with 10–20 at.% HCP-forming elements (e.g., Ti or Zr). Perform standardized room-temperature compression and tension tests to measure yield strength and plastic strain. Supplement mechanical tests with electron microscopy to analyze dislocation core structure and slip system activation.
measurements: Phase analysis (XRD) to confirm single-phase microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the test alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvement in ductility (or displays reduced yield strength without compensatory plasticity improvement) compared to the control BCC alloy, or if the dislocation mechanisms remain unchanged, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. One such class comprises the RHEAs which, because of their high melting points, have been proposed as candidates for ultrahigh-temperature applications. However, a single-phase RHEA, TiZrHfNbTa, was recently shown to be significantly weaker in creep than CMSX-4 despite the former’s higher melting point. The weakness was ascribed to two factors: faster diffusion in the BCC matrix of the RHEA relative to the FCC matrix of CMSX-4 and a lack of precipitates. Additional research is therefore needed to enhance the creep strength of TiZrHfNbTa, for example, by the introduction of suitable strengthening precipitates. Meanwhile, RHEAs with higher melting points must also be investigated since diffusion will be slower in such materials. One such RHEA is VNbMoTaW, whose melting point is ~500 °C higher than TiZrHfNbTa,,. However, it has a major disadvantage: lack of ductility at room temperature even in compression.
